section_title: Why does the same word produce different responses?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 4 While a large crowd was gathering and people were coming to Jesus from town after town, He told them this parable: 5 “A farmer went out to sow his seed. And as he was sowing, some seed fell along the path, where it was trampled, and the birds of the air devoured it. 6 Some fell on rocky ground, and when it came up, the seedlings withered because they had no moisture. 7 Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up with it and choked the seedlings. 8 Still other seed fell on good soil, where it sprang up and produced a crop—a hundredfold.” As Jesus said this, He called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

9 Then His disciples asked Him what this parable meant. 10 He replied, “The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to others I speak in parables, so that, ‘though seeing, they may not see; though hearing, they may not understand.’

11 Now this is the meaning of the parable: The seed is the word of God. 12 The seeds along the path are those who hear, but the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. 13 The seeds on rocky ground are those who hear the word and receive it with joy, but they have no root. They believe for a season, but in the time of testing, they fall away. 14 The seeds that fell among the thorns are those who hear, but as they go on their way, they are choked by the worries, riches, and pleasures of this life, and their fruit does not mature. 15 But the seeds on good soil are those with a noble and good heart, who hear the word, cling to it, and by persevering produce a crop.

context_lines: People come to Jesus from many towns, and He tells a story about a farmer sowing seed. Some falls on a path, some on rocky ground, some among thorns and some on good soil. The outcomes differ: the seed is eaten, the seedlings wither, the growth is choked, or a crop is produced.

When the disciples ask what the story means, Jesus says that knowledge of the kingdom’s mysteries has been given to them. His words about seeing without seeing and hearing without understanding echo Isaiah’s commission. The parable involves both the gift of understanding and a serious warning about hearing. ([Isaiah 6:9–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/6.htm))

Jesus identifies the seed as God’s word and explains the different responses. The devil takes away the word from the first hearers. The rocky-ground hearers receive it joyfully but have no root; they believe for a time and fall away under testing. Worries, riches and pleasures choke the response of others so that their fruit does not mature.

The good-soil hearers keep hold of the word and produce a crop through perseverance. The explanation asks more than whether someone has heard a message or welcomed it at first. It draws attention to what happens to that word over time.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readings commonly see different responses to God’s word and a call to lasting, fruitful hearing. Traditions differ over how God’s gift of understanding relates to the hearer’s response, and over what happens when someone who believed later turns away.

Reformed teaching in Westminster emphasizes God renewing the heart and will so that people freely come to Christ. Wesley’s notes on the Matthew parallel emphasize people refusing to use the light already given and closing their eyes to it. The Catholic Catechism describes the parables as confronting hearers with a choice and calls them to become disciples who receive the kingdom’s meaning. These emphases all recognize the need for God’s grace. ([Westminster Confession 10.1–2](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html); [Wesley on Matthew 13:11–16](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-matthew/); [Catechism 546](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P1L.HTM))

On continuing in faith, the Westminster Confession and the 1689 Baptist Confession teach that God keeps those He has brought to saving faith to the end, though they can fall into serious sin for a time. This gives Reformed Christians and Baptists who follow that confession a way of distinguishing temporary response from saving faith that endures. ([Westminster Confession 17.1–3](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html); [1689 Baptist Confession 17.1–3](https://www.the1689confession.com/1689/chapter-17))

The Methodist Articles allow for departing from grace and falling into sin after receiving the Holy Spirit, with repentance and return possible by grace. The Catholic Church teaches that faith is God’s free gift, that it can be lost and that it must be nourished. These teachings lead to different explanations of whether someone who abandons faith once had saving faith. ([Methodist Articles of Religion, XII](https://www.umc.org/en/content/articles-of-religion); [Catechism 162](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_one/chapter_three/article_1/iii_the_characteristics_of_faith.html))
god_plan_lines: The Isaiah passage Jesus echoes also appears near the end of Acts. Paul speaks about Jesus and God’s kingdom; some are convinced and others refuse to believe. He then cites Isaiah and announces that God’s salvation has been sent to the nations. The repeated connection places the mixed response to the word within the gospel’s widening journey. ([Acts 28:23–28](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/28.htm))

Peter uses the picture of seed to describe new birth through God’s living and enduring word, then identifies that word with the good news proclaimed to his readers. This is a related picture, not a second code for assigning each soil to a group. It connects the message Jesus describes here with the life God brings through the gospel. ([1 Peter 1:22–25](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/1.htm))
